title: What's actually inside India's inflation basket?
tension: The single inflation number is a giant weighted average of hundreds of things, from rice to rent to a child's school fees, and the way they are weighted decides whose life the number describes. Two ideas do all the work and people constantly confuse them: how much a thing weighs in the basket, and how much it is actually contributing to this month's inflation. A small-weight item with a price spike can drive the headline; a heavy item going nowhere can sit silent. Decode the basket and you stop being fooled by the headline.
teachingGoal: Open up the CPI from the top down: headline to the six groups to their sub-groups to individual items, so a reader sees exactly what is being measured. Crucially, teach the difference between a component's WEIGHT (its share of the basket) and its CONTRIBUTION (how much it is adding to current inflation), and why a small-weight item can swing the headline while a heavy one stays quiet. Ground it in real Indian items: cereals, vegetables, pulses, oils, milk, eggs, plus health, education and transport.
sectionArc: Where does the single inflation number come from? (it is a weighted average of a fixed basket; the major divisions and their weights in the current 2024 basket, shown as a stacked bar; food the largest at about 37%)

Wait, didn't the basket just change? Decode the 2026 revision (the new 2024 base launched in February 2026; food's weight fell from 45.86% to 36.75% as Indians spend more on services; new items like OTT, e-commerce and telecom data; the reweighting itself is Engel's law made visible)

Weight versus contribution: the distinction that trips everyone up (weight is the share of the basket; contribution is how much a group is adding to this month's inflation; show how they differ when a group's own inflation is high or negative)
Inside food and beverages: the sub-groups that move (cereals, vegetables, pulses, oils and fats, milk and products; their index levels and how differently they behave)
The volatile few: items that spike (vegetables, pulses, edible oils, eggs, sugar; why these swing far more than the average and grab headlines)
Inside 'miscellaneous': the modern, sticky costs (health, education, transport and communication, personal care; the slow, steady services inflation hiding behind the food noise)
Why a small slice can move the whole number (a high-inflation item with a small weight can contribute more than a big, flat one; worked through the contribution figures)
So how should you read the basket? (look past the headline to which groups and items are actually driving it, and ask whether they are yours)
mustTeach: the headline CPI is a weighted average of a fixed basket of goods and services, grouped into six broad heads
a component's WEIGHT (share of the basket) is different from its CONTRIBUTION (how much it adds to current inflation)
food and beverages splits into sub-groups (cereals, vegetables, pulses, oils, milk) that behave very differently
a few items (vegetables, pulses, oils, eggs) are far more volatile than the average and dominate headlines
the 'miscellaneous' group hides steady services inflation (health, education, transport) that is stickier than food
a small-weight, high-inflation item can drive the headline more than a heavy, flat one

CURRENCY (important): the current official basket is the 2024-base series, launched 12 Feb 2026. Use the 2024 weights (food and beverages 36.75%) as the CURRENT weights, and cite the old 2012 weights only to show what changed. The detailed month-by-month component inflation figures (vegetables, onion, etc.) come from the longer 2012-base series and must be framed as recent readings under the previous basket, never invented for the new base.

contextCards.fact: A price index combines many items into one number using fixed weights drawn from how a representative household spends. The contribution of a group to inflation in a given month is roughly its weight multiplied by its own inflation rate, which is why a heavy group with near-zero inflation can contribute little, while a lighter group with a sharp price rise can contribute a lot. Weight is about the basket; contribution is about the moment.

On 12 February 2026 India launched a new Consumer Price Index series with base year 2024 (replacing 2012), built on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023-24. The biggest change: the weight of food and beverages fell from 45.86% to 36.75%, because Indians now spend a smaller share of their budgets on food and more on services, a textbook case of Engel's law. Housing and utilities rose to about 17.7%, transport and communication to about 12.4%, and health to about 6.1%. The basket grew from 299 to 358 items, adding e-commerce and online prices, telecom data plans and OTT streaming subscriptions for the first time, and switched to the international COICOP classification of 12 divisions instead of the old six groups. Headline inflation on the new base was 2.75% in January 2026.
